title: Self-Driving Cars
resolution: Resolved: The federal government should allow fully driverless vehicles on public roads nationwide.
summary: Driverless taxis already carry passengers in several U.S. cities under state rules. Should national rules open roads everywhere to them?

background.p: Companies such as Waymo operate fully driverless ride services in several U.S. cities, under a patchwork of state and local rules. Waymo's peer-reviewed analysis of about 7.1 million driverless miles in Phoenix, San Francisco and Los Angeles through October 2023 found about 85% fewer injury-reported crashes than a human-driver benchmark, while noting the benchmarks are imprecise and some comparisons were not statistically significant.

Setbacks have shaped the debate: in October 2023, California suspended Cruise's driverless permit after one of its cars dragged a pedestrian who had been struck by another vehicle, and the company later ended its robotaxi business. A frequently quoted claim that "94% of serious crashes are due to human error" comes from a 2015 federal memo that assigned the last event before a crash to the driver; the head of the National Transportation Safety Board called the statistic misleading in 2022, and the agency said it would reword it.

disputed.q: Are driverless cars safer than human drivers?
positions: Company data from millions of miles show far fewer injury crashes than human benchmarks in the cities studied.
Critics note the data come mostly from the companies, cover limited cities and conditions, and compare against imprecise human baselines.

terms.def: A vehicle that can drive itself in some or all conditions.
A vehicle that drives itself with no human needed, but only within certain areas or conditions.
The specific places and conditions where a self-driving system is designed to work.
When federal law overrides state or local law on the same subject.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Driverless vehicles can save lives and widen mobility, and one national framework is better than a patchwork.

args.claim: Driverless cars may be safer than human drivers.
args.warrant: Automated systems don't drink, text, get tired or speed on purpose, which are major factors in serious crashes.
args.evidence: Waymo's peer-reviewed comparison (85% fewer injury-reported crashes over 7.1 million miles); NHTSA crash data on impairment and distraction.
args.response: The negative answers that the data come mostly from the company, from a few cities with good weather, and the benchmarks are imprecise.

args.claim: They can give mobility to people who can't drive.
args.warrant: Older adults, people with disabilities and people without cars could travel independently.
args.evidence: Census and transportation data on non-drivers; disability-advocacy reports on driverless service.
args.response: The negative replies that most driverless service is in dense cities, so rural non-drivers may not benefit for years.

args.claim: A national framework beats a patchwork.
args.warrant: When rules differ by state and city, companies can't scale, and safety standards vary. One federal standard can be stricter and clearer.
args.evidence: Comparisons of state AV laws; federal motor vehicle safety standards as a model.
args.response: The negative argues states and cities know their roads, and federal preemption could block local safety rules.

args.claim: Waiting has a cost in lives.
args.warrant: If a safer technology is held back, people continue to die in crashes it might have prevented.
args.evidence: NHTSA annual traffic death counts; safety analyses of AV performance.
args.response: The negative replies that rushing an unproven technology everywhere risks new kinds of crashes and public backlash.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Driverless cars should expand step by step under local oversight until safety is proven across conditions.

args.warrant: Results in sunny cities don't show how the cars handle snow, rural roads or unusual events, so national approval is premature.
args.evidence: Waymo's own note that benchmarks are imprecise and results limited to certain cities; reports on AV performance in rare situations.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the resolution can include conditions; federal approval can still require testing for each area.

args.claim: Failures can be new and serious.
args.warrant: Automated systems can fail in ways no human would, and accountability is unclear when no one is driving.
args.evidence: California's 2023 suspension of Cruise's permit after a pedestrian was dragged; NHTSA investigations of AV incidents.
args.response: The affirmative replies that regulators acted quickly, showing oversight works, and that human crashes are far more common.

args.claim: Local governments need control over their streets.
args.warrant: Cities manage traffic, emergency response and street use; nationwide permission could stop them from setting limits that fit local conditions.
args.evidence: City officials' complaints about AVs blocking emergency vehicles; state and city regulatory disputes.
args.response: The affirmative argues national safety rules can leave room for local traffic management.

args.claim: Jobs for millions of drivers are at stake.
args.warrant: Truck, taxi and delivery drivers could lose work quickly if driverless vehicles spread nationwide before workers can adjust.
args.evidence: Bureau of Labor Statistics data on driving occupations; labor union statements.
args.response: The affirmative replies that adoption will take years, and new jobs in maintenance and operations will appear.

strawmen.strawman: They want to let robots drive kids to school with no testing.
strawmen.why: Supporters favor national safety standards and point to millions of tested miles.
strawmen.steelman: Driverless cars appear far safer than human drivers where they operate, can help people who can't drive, and need one clear national framework.

strawmen.strawman: They're just afraid of new technology.
strawmen.why: Opponents point to limited data, real failures and the need for local control.
strawmen.steelman: Safety hasn't been shown across all conditions, failures can be new and serious, and cities need control, so expansion should be gradual and local.

weak.arg: 94% of crashes are caused by human error, so driverless cars will prevent 94% of crashes.
weak.why: The NTSB called that statistic misleading, and it doesn't follow that machines would avoid all those crashes.

weak.arg: Self-driving cars will be hacked and used as weapons.
weak.why: A speculative worst case without evidence; cybersecurity is a fair point, but argue it with evidence.

aff: Where did Waymo's miles come from, and in what weather?
neg: What did Waymo's peer-reviewed study find about injury crashes?
How many people die on U.S. roads each year?
What evidence would convince you to allow driverless cars more widely?
